extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy; readers of Kant
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Kantian criteria for judging the moral worth of actions and the form of moral law: universality, purity of motive, exclusion of empirical incentives, and the subjective feeling of respect. Aimed at assessing maxims and wills according to the Groundwork's practical reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good will (will conforming to a practical a priori law)
rubrics_metrics.description: "a will whose maxim always conforms to this law is good absolutely in every respect and is the supreme condition of all good."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a rational principle is conceived as of itself the determining principle of the will (without regard to possible objects of desire), then that principle is a practical a priori law and pure reason is practical of itself. The law determines the will directly; the action conformed to it is good in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodness relative to inclination (empirical goodness)
rubrics_metrics.description: When "the maxim of the will is consequent on a determining principle of desire which presupposes an object of pleasure or pain... the action... is good relatively to our inclination... the will whose maxim is affected thereby is not a pure will."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maxims grounded in desires or empirical ends may be rational practical precepts but are not laws; their goodness is only relative (welfare, empirical concept), not absolute. Such maxims cannot be called pure laws and the corresponding will is not 'pure'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological priority of the moral law
rubrics_metrics.description: "the concept of good and evil must not be determined before the moral law... but only after it and by means of it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not begin ethical inquiry by positing an object (e.g., happiness, perfection) as the foundation of the law; instead first investigate whether there is a pure a priori determining principle of the will (a moral law). Beginning from an empirical object forecloses the possibility of a pure practical law and yields heteronomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formality and universality of the moral law
rubrics_metrics.description: Only "a formal law — that is, one which prescribes to reason nothing more than the form of its universal legislation as the supreme condition of its maxims — that can be a priori a determining principle of practical reason."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moral law must prescribe the form of universal legislation (universalisability) rather than content tied to contingent ends. Principles that make the object (pleasure, happiness, God's will) the determining ground imply heteronomy and empirical conditions and therefore fail as pure moral laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of freedom (typology for assessing maxims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Table headings: I. Quantity (subjective according to maxims; objective according to principles; a priori both objective and subjective principles of freedom (laws)). II. Quality (practical rules of action (praeceptivae); rules of omission (prohibitivae); rules of exceptions (exceptivae)). III. Relation (to personality; to the condition of the person; reciprocal). IV. Modality (The Permitted and the Forbidden; Duty and the contrary to duty; Perfect and imperfect duty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories as a systematic scheme to classify and survey maxims and practical questions: whether a maxim is subjective/objective, whether it prescribes action or omission, the relational scope (person/condition/reciprocity), and the modal status (permitted/forbidden/duty; perfect vs imperfect duties). This organizes what must be answered in practical philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universalizability test (typic of the moral law)
rubrics_metrics.description: "ask yourself whether, if the action you propose were to take place by a law of the system of nature of which you were yourself a part, you could regard it as possible by your own will."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a maxim by imagining it as a law of nature applying universally; if the maxim could not coherently be willed as such a universal law, then it is morally impossible. This is the practical judgement's rule for applying abstract law to a concrete action (the form of a universal law is the test).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral worth requires acting from duty (the moral law as direct determinant)
rubrics_metrics.description: "What is essential in the moral worth of actions is that the moral law should directly determine the will. If the determination of the will takes place... only by means of a feeling... then the action will possess legality, but not morality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an action to have moral worth its immediate (subjective) motive must be the moral law itself (acting from duty). Actions that merely conform to duty because of feelings, incentives, or inclinations have legal correctness but lack genuine moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of sensible impulses from the determining principle
rubrics_metrics.description: "being a free will it is determined simply by the moral law, not only without the co-operation of sensible impulses, but even to the rejection of all such, and to the checking of all inclinations so far as they might be opposed to that law."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A free will determined by the moral law must exclude or check all inclinations and sensible impulses that would oppose the law. The moral law's effect is negative (it thwarts inclinations, producing feelings like pain/humiliation) and thereby creates the proper subjective condition for law-based action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for the moral law as a non-empirical motive/effect
rubrics_metrics.description: "respect for the moral law is a feeling which is produced by an intellectual cause, and this feeling is the only one that we know quite a priori..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect is a practical feeling produced by pure practical reason (an intellectual effect) rather than an empirical feeling. It arises when the moral law humbles self-conceit and removes obstacles to reason's causality; while not an antecedent empirical motive, it functions subjectively to give authority to the law and conduce to acting from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect applies to persons, not things (distinguish respect from admiration)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Respect applies always to persons only- not to things... Admiration... can apply to things also... But all this is not respect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing moral attitudes, distinguish respect (a reaction to moral law/persons exemplifying law that humbles self-conceit) from admiration or astonishment directed at things or talents. True respect responds to the moral worth or law-exemplifying person and may persist even when one recognizes the person's imperfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject empiricism as the foundation of moral law
rubrics_metrics.description: "empiricism of practical reason, which founds the practical notions of good and evil merely on experienced consequences (so-called happiness)... Empiricism... cuts up at the roots the morality of intentions... and substitutes for duty something quite different, namely, an empirical interest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid grounding moral principles in empirical consequences (happiness, feelings). Such grounding renders moral principles heteronomous and allied to inclinations; it undermines duty and the purity of moral intentions. The proper approach is rationalism of judgement: using the sensible system only as a formal type and preserving a priori demand for conformity to law.
